FEMA conspiracy theories spreading through hurricane-affected communities after a disaster are not new. Grief, anger, and genuine institutional failure create fertile ground for them. What is new, or at least newly documented, is the degree to which that ground is being deliberately seeded. The Institute for Strategic Dialogue has published an assessment of a Russian disinformation campaign specifically targeting U.S. government hurricane response. The timing is June 2026. The method is familiar if you've been paying attention, and it's worth walking through carefully because the mechanics matter. The operation isn't one thing. It's layered. There's the amplification of FEMA conspiracy theories, specifically ones alleging that disaster relief is being deliberately withheld or misallocated. The communities being targeted are already dealing with loss, and already inclined toward frustration with slow or inadequate federal response, because slow and inadequate federal response is a real thing that happens. The disinformation doesn't have to invent a crisis. It just has to find the gap between what people expected and what they got, and widen it. Then there's false attribution: fabricated or decontextualized statements attributed to FEMA officials and other emergency management figures. This is an old tool but a durable one. A fake quote doesn't need to travel far before it becomes a screenshot, and a screenshot doesn't need a source. By the time anyone checks, the impression is set. There are narratives designed to exploit racial and class divisions around disaster response. Again, this isn't fantasy material. The history of U.S. disaster response along racial and socioeconomic lines is genuinely uneven, and anyone who lived through Katrina or its aftermath doesn't need to be convinced of that. The operation finds that real grievance and amplifies it into something that erodes trust not just in one agency or one administration but in the basic premise that the government is acting in good faith toward particular communities. That's the target: not FEMA specifically, but institutional legitimacy broadly. And alongside all of that, there's comparative framing. Russian emergency management held up as a contrast, idealized or outright fabricated, to construct a Russia-versus-America narrative in which the United States comes out looking neglectful and corrupt. This part is almost comical in its transparency if you know to look for it, but most people encountering these narratives organically don't have the context to notice. The strategic logic here is not subtle once you see it. Democratic governance runs on public trust in a fairly basic way. People need to believe that institutions are attempting to act in their interest, even when they fail, for those institutions to function. What Russian information operations do in moments like this is collapse the distinction between legitimate criticism and coordinated attack. When someone raises a real concern about FEMA resource allocation, and that concern is indistinguishable from a piece of a foreign influence operation, something corrosive happens. Genuine accountability becomes harder. Communities trying to process real failures are handed a distorted lens. And the people running the operation don't care which concerns are authentic, because the goal isn't accuracy. It's noise. It's the feeling that nothing can be trusted, including the people trying to tell you something can't be trusted. ISD notes that this approach mirrors what was documented during COVID-19, when Russian operations consistently identified moments of peak government credibility vulnerability and concentrated disinformation resources there. Public health, social justice events, now disaster response. The throughline is opportunism applied to institutional stress fractures. You don't create the fracture. You find it and you work it. The timing situates this within a broader information offensive ahead of the 2026 midterms, consistent with the 2026 Annual Threat Assessment's documentation of Russian efforts to degrade U.S. institutional trust across multiple domains simultaneously. That's not a coincidence or a hypothesis. It's a documented pattern playing out on schedule. Here is where the situation gets genuinely uncomfortable. The primary U.S. government mechanism for identifying and countering foreign disinformation operations, the State Department's foreign misinformation countermeasures infrastructure, was shut down in February 2026. Gone. Which means that an ISD report like this one is doing work that used to be done, in part, by the U.S. government itself. The platform trust and safety teams trying to catch coordinated inauthentic behavior, the researchers flagging manipulated content, the journalists writing about it: they're operating without the institutional backstop that used to exist. That's not a small thing. Russian operations targeting hurricane response in an election year are not a niche concern. The communities being targeted are real. Some of them are still in FEMA trailers. Some of them are navigating appeals processes for aid they haven't received. They are being told, through coordinated foreign channels, that the system doesn't just fail them by accident. That it fails them on purpose. By design. Because of who they are. The ISD assessment is useful. Read it. The Docket and the Ballot Marc Elias 10:03 PM Thursday, June 25 No one issue has defined Donald Trump's political movement more than the war over who votes and how. And nothing is more central to that war than mail-in voting. In the run-up to 2020, Trump spread lies about mail-in voting. When he lost, he attacked it in court. The violence of Jan. 6, 2021, was fueled as much by conspiracy theories about mail-in ballots as by the bizarre claims about rigged machines and dead foreign leaders. The attacks never stopped. The press may occasionally claim that the Republican Party has embraced mail-in voting. I can tell you with certainty that is not true. Over the last six years, I have litigated more cases to protect mail-in voting than I can count. Inevitably, the GOP is on the opposing side. Right now, the Supreme Court is weighing Watson v. RNC — a challenge to states' practice of counting ballots postmarked by Election Day but arriving days later. If the RNC wins, hundreds of thousands of lawful votes will be thrown out. This follows a wave of Republican state legislative efforts to ban or limit ballot drop boxes, shorten windows to request and return ballots, and add technical requirements designed to increase rejection rates. As the 2026 midterms approach, Trump has recognized that this is not enough. He is too unpopular and his party too damaged. So he has escalated — weaponizing his administration, inspiring more outlandish lies among his supporters. But once again, Trump is growing frustrated. His efforts to enact the SAVE Act have failed. His redistricting scheme came up short. Most importantly, his efforts to use the government to rig elections are being blocked in court. I fear something is going to break, and the results could be devastating. We are watching an administration that has shown no respect for court orders it dislikes, a postmaster general who serves at Trump's pleasure and is willing to do his bidding. Most importantly, Trump has already demonstrated he will invite violence when legal options are exhausted. The 2026 midterms are only four months away. The attacks on voting — and in particular mail-in voting — are happening now and getting worse. Earlier this year, Trump signed an executive order directing the Department of Homeland Security to create a master list of citizens eligible to vote in each state, and instructed the U.S. Postal Service not to deliver absentee ballots to any voter not on a state-approved list. States that refused to comply would lose federal funding. Lawsuits followed immediately. I sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., on behalf of the Democratic Party. Democratic attorneys general from 23 states sued in Massachusetts. Various non-profits sued as well. This week, the federal judge in the attorneys general's case issued a sweeping ruling blocking Trump's order — prohibiting the administration from creating a federal program to control state voter rolls and barring the Postal Service from withholding ballots from voters. While the ruling directly protects voters in only those 23 states, it may derail the Postal Service rulemaking altogether, since mail crosses state lines and the administration faces additional legal challenges that could produce a nationwide injunction. This is part of a broader losing streak for Donald Trump. Separately, this week, another federal court rejected the Justice Department's efforts to access state voter files. This brings the DOJ's record in these cases to 0-9. My law firm is fighting the DOJ in all 31 cases in which it seeks this information. We are undefeated. Of the nine cases DOJ has lost, five have been before judges nominated by Trump. Equally important, this week the 6th Circuit became the first appeals court to affirm a lower court victory in these cases. While other cases at the trial and appellate court remain, I am more confident than ever that we will block the DOJ's efforts to seize vital citizen voting information. But the fight is far from over. I have written before about Trump's pattern of escalation: First, lie about elections. Next, bully opponents. Then, sue. When the courts rule against him, he escalates to violence. We saw this in 2020. We saw it when he targeted migrants in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minnesota. And it is what he is planning for 2026. This does not undo the significance of the court victories. In fact, it makes them essential. Blocking Trump's access to sensitive voter data protects citizens. Preventing his postmaster general from cutting off mail-in voting protects elections. Blocking the SAVE Act protects democracy. I have spent six years in courtrooms fighting for the right of Americans to cast their ballots by mail. We have won more than we have lost and more than people thought we would. Those victories have come in state and federal courts, including the Supreme Court. But I will tell you that winning in court is not enough. Court cases can give citizens the right to vote, but do not ensure that they do. They can make sure ballots are cast and counted, but not that the results are accepted by Republicans who lose. The victories matter. We must keep winning them. But we still need voters to vote as if the future of democracy is not only on the docket but on the ballot.
